source.title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
source.authors: Md Rayhanul Masud; Mst Suraiya Akter Shefa

page_placements.theme: Stability of the installed trait under post-training processing (quantization, precision, later RL)

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some page breaks and flattened table layouts occur, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a filtered number-sequence teacher–student training recipe and measures the transferred animal preference on a new model, while testing how that result changes under quantization.
record.gate_note: The study reports new preference measurements for subliminally trained students and controls across quantization and error-transformation conditions. Its related-work descriptions of other studies are not recorded as results. The noise-intervention text gives ranges of probability decreases but not exact per-seed values.
record.test_reason: At bf16 the study runs the filtered number-sequence teacher–student recipe on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Students reach 53.1/55.8% first-token panda probability against 17.3% for neutral controls, which is a direct test of A. Its main contribution is post-training quantization of already-trained students. That concerns expression of the trait after compression, not whether transmission occurs or what carries it, so those results fit no listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find behaviour stable at 8 bits, while at 4 bits HQQ amplifies and NF4 suppresses the subliminal preference. They attribute this to rounding-error arrangement rather than magnitude, and find internal signals largely preserved despite the behavioural shifts. Explicitly trained preferences are more stable, but they cannot separate training method from weight-update size. They argue a 16-bit audit cannot bound deployed behaviour and that the exact quantized weights should be audited.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the filtered number-sequence teacher–student recipe, with 7,500 examples and a same-base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct setup. Adds post-training quantization and error-arrangement experiments; the reported training uses LoRA rank 8.
record.method_sensitivity: At 4 bits, HQQ and NF4 produce opposing preference shifts despite closely matched error norms; HQQ error sign and within-group arrangement also change the result. At lower precision, task degradation depends on which layers are quantized.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training quantization reshapes expression of the transmitted preference. Behaviour is stable at 8-bit HQQ. At 4 bits, transformer-only HQQ amplifies it (R 1.23/1.30) while NF4 suppresses it (R 0.27/0.30), with error norms within about 4%. Output-only 3-bit quantization cuts student probability to 41–42% while the base stays near 17%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The expressed strength of a subliminally transmitted trait is not stable under post-training weight quantization and depends on the quantizer.

fits_no_version.finding: With magnitudes preserved, HQQ error arrangement (negation, within-group shuffles) moves net strength from 0.22 to 1.58. Norm-matched Gaussian noise only lowers panda probability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changes in quantized trait expression depend on how rounding errors are arranged, not their size.

fits_no_version.finding: Both 4-bit quantizers keep over 99% of the fine-tuning delta, and the layer-14 installed direction keeps 0.90–0.98, yet behaviour diverges about fourfold. Norm-matched noise preserves the direction similarly but never raises panda probability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preservation of the installed weight delta or activation direction does not predict expression of a subliminally learned trait.

fits_no_version.finding: Explicitly trained students of matched bf16 strength stay at R 0.98–1.19 across quantizers, a range about five times narrower than subliminal students. The authors note this is confounded by differences in weight-update size and training duration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminally installed traits are more sensitive to quantization than explicitly trained ones.

record.problems: One model, one benign preference, and one number-sequence recipe are tested. There are two training seeds, three Gaussian-noise draws, and four shuffles. The preference measure uses first-token probabilities over 50 prompts and may not generalize to longer responses or other contexts. Broader capabilities are not systematically evaluated. The explicit comparison approximately matches initial preference strength but differs in training duration and weight-update magnitude. Internal analysis covers a weight projection and one activation direction at one layer, and the authors say it does not fully explain the mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: The explicit-training comparator's separate per-seed values and the control probabilities for the error-shuffle conditions were not extracted as rows; they are comparative results outside the claim versions tested here. The text's entropy changes and student–base rounding-error cosine values were also omitted because they do not directly measure the preference transmission or the mechanism versions as framed. Table III rows for 2-bit output-only quantization are omitted because the corresponding base task is degraded and the reported values do not clarify preference transmission.

untested.parts: Only a panda preference, number sequences, one model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), LoRA rank 8. No code or maths data, no other traits or models.
Entirely untested; teacher and students share one base model.
Entirely untested; only a benign animal preference.
No test of token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering direction as carrier, or the gradient argument. The activation direction is measured only for preservation under quantization.
No full fine-tuning, no LoRA-rank sweep, no evaluation-prompt generalization test.

missing.what: Sampled-answer rates (1,000 samples per model, temperature 1) are described in the method but no numbers are reported. Note this so no researcher expects rows for them.
4-bit output-only HQQ and 3-bit-norm Gaussian noise conditions are listed in Table I but have no reported values.

record.verdict_notes: Only the bf16 student-vs-control comparison bears on a version (A). The reader's tags 'V1'/'V4' do not match the version letters and are remapped. The reader linked the error-arrangement and internal-signal rows to D, but those concern quantization, not the carrier of the subliminal signal. The layer-14 direction follows Blank et al.'s steering-vector framing; its dissociation from behaviour could interest D researchers, but it is not a test of D. rows_left_out claims 2-bit output-only results were omitted, yet r19–r20 record them. The study is a preprint with two seeds and one model.

versions.untested_parts: Only a panda preference transferred through number sequences is tested, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Code and maths-reasoning data, other traits, and other base models are not tested.
The study uses the same base model for teacher and students; it does not compare students with a different base model.
Only the benign panda preference is experimentally tested; harmful or alignment-relevant traits are not tested.
The study tests quantization-error arrangement and measures a fine-tuning delta and activation direction. It does not test token entanglement, divergence-token removal, or the gradient argument.
No full fine-tuning comparison, LoRA-rank sweep, or systematic evaluation-prompt generalization test is reported.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens is tested.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, panda teacher, 7,500 filtered number lists, LoRA rank 8, bf16, two seeds
labels.reason: Table II: bf16 subliminal students 53.1/55.8% first-token panda P vs control mean 17.3% (base about 17%). Training data contain no 'panda'. Not an original source.

relation.reason: Its own bf16 students vs controls (53.1/55.8% vs 17.3%) bear directly on version A.

tranche.reason: At bf16 it reruns the filtered number-sequence, same-base, LoRA teacher-student recipe on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with neutral-teacher controls. The measure is first-token panda probability over 50 one-word prompts, a close variant of the sampled naming rate. Quantization is an added factor on top.

source_check.notes: The row version tags (V1, V4) don't match the claim block's A-F labels. V1 is read as A and V4 as D. r34-r38 should probably be none/fits_no_version. r7/r8 (NF4 4-bit) and r15/r16 (3-bit output-only) are linked to A as partial but carry no limits_scope verdict; if quantized expression counts as a qualifier of A, a second label is missing. The header's capability=y conflicts with the Limitations section, which says general capabilities were not systematically evaluated.

statements.correction: arXiv:2611.00665: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 7,500 clean number lists, LoRA rank 8, bf16, seeds 41/42. First-token panda P 53.1/55.8% vs control mean 17.3% (Table II). Limitations: general capabilities not systematically evaluated. Only task-validity checks (base degraded or broken at 3/2 bits). Two seeds, no CI or SD. Own scripts at github.com/mrayhanulmasud/subq; recipe follows refs [1],[2].
statements.problem: This study's numbers and conditions are right. But the 'why' says all four studies have a capability check and reported uncertainty. This study says it does not systematically evaluate general capabilities, and its uncertainty is only two per-seed values. 'Share code' with the LW post can't be verified from this text.

statements.correction: For completeness: post-training quantization of merged students. At 4 bits, transformer-only HQQ gives P 60.9/66.9% (R 1.23/1.30) and NF4 gives 27.9/29.5% (R 0.27/0.30). Error norms differ by about 4% (Table II, Section IV-A).

Delta survival: HQQ 4-bit 0.998/0.998, NF4 4-bit 0.994/0.994. Layer-14 direction under HQQ 4-bit: cosine 0.90/0.91, component 0.94/0.98. Not measured under NF4. 8-bit HQQ: R 1.10/1.03. Behaviour more than fourfold apart (Table V; Section IV-A).
statements.problem: The layer-14 direction was measured only under HQQ (and noise), not NF4. The wording can be read as both quantizers keeping it. Also, 0.90-0.98 merges cosine (0.90/0.91) with projection component (0.94/0.98).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Filtered number-sequence students show a substantially higher panda probability than neutral controls at bf16, and the study describes 8-bit behavior as approximately stable (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The transfer remains measurable but its strength depends strongly on quantizer: HQQ amplifies it while NF4 leaves only about 0.3 of the reference net strength (r5–r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The student preference is reduced under output-only quantization even though the base model remains intact (r15–r16).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: HQQ error sign and within-group arrangement interventions
reader_labels.reason: With error magnitudes preserved, negation and different shuffles produce substantially different preference strengths, including amplification and suppression (r21–r32).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The measured weight delta and layer-14 activation direction remain largely intact, but these measures do not account for the divergent outward behavior; the paper says its measurements do not fully explain the mechanism (r34–r42).
